lead: Memory arrays fail in ways random logic does not. A write to one cell can disturb its neighbour, a cell can refuse to change, and the address decoder can select no cell, two cells or the wrong cell. Vectors built for stuck-at faults in logic miss these, so memories are tested with ordered read and write sequences called march tests. The same tests run at wafer sort, at final test and inside the chip through memory BIST.
prereq: You need: the SRAM cell, the row and column decoders and the sense amplifier, from the memory chapters, and stuck-at faults from 6.2.

sections.h3: Fault models the test must excite

blocks.text: For test, a memory is five blocks: the address decoder, the cell array, the sense amplifiers, the write drivers and the read/write control. The cells sit in a dense grid, so one cell can disturb a neighbour; the decoder is a tree of gates, so a bad address line can open no word, two words or the wrong word. In this chapter the memory is bit-oriented: n is the number of addresses, each holding one bit.

head: Fault model
Meaning
rows: The cell always reads 0, or always reads 1.
A write to an aggressor cell changes a victim cell: an inversion CF flips it, an idempotent CF forces it to a value; a state CF needs the aggressor only to hold a value.
An address reaches no cell, several cells, or the wrong cell.
A cell's value depends on the pattern held in the cells around it.
A cell loses its data after a pause, or without refresh in DRAM.

blocks.text: A coupling fault always has an aggressor and a victim. To excite it, the test must first give the victim a known value, then write the aggressor with the right transition, then read the victim. Because the aggressor can sit above or below the victim in the address space, the test needs passes in both address orders.

A march test is a list of march elements. Each element visits every address in one order and does the same operations at each. ⇑ means ascending address order, ⇓ descending, and ⇕ either. w0 and w1 write 0 and 1; r0 and r1 read and expect 0 and 1, and a mismatch is a fail.

head: Test
Elements
Length
rows: write and read a 0101… pattern, then its inverse
one base cell holds the odd value while all others are read
every base cell is read against every other cell

blocks.text: The length of a march test is k × n, where k is the number of operations in all its elements. March C− has 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 10 and detects stuck-at, transition, address decoder faults and the unlinked inversion and idempotent coupling faults. MATS+ costs only 5n but misses many coupling faults. Walking and GALPAT grow with n², so a 1 Mbit array would need trillions of operations; they are used on small arrays or for diagnosis.

sections.h3: Memory BIST and the logic around the array

blocks.text: Memory BIST puts the march engine on the chip. Its controller holds:

items: a sequencer that steps through the march elements and their operations;
an address counter that counts up or down;
a data generator that supplies the write data and the expected read data (all 0s, all 1s, or a background such as a checkerboard for word-wide memories);
a comparator that checks every read and sets a fail flag, and can record the failing address;
a multiplexer at the memory ports that switches the array between functional logic and BIST.

blocks.text: One controller can serve many memories, testing them in parallel to save time or one after another to limit power; that choice is the BIST controller configuration. The logic around the memory (port multiplexers, byte enables, ECC, address and data wrap logic) also needs testing: through scan, or by running BIST through it. Algorithmic optimisation picks the shortest march that still covers the fault list the product needs, and large memories add spare rows and columns that a repair step, built-in self-repair, switches in after BIST reports the failures.

examples.question: A 1024-address bit-oriented SRAM is tested with March C−. Count the operations per address and the total accesses. At 5 ns per access, find the test time. Compare it with GALPAT at about 4n² accesses.
steps: Operations per address: ⇕(w0) 1, ⇑(r0, w1) 2, ⇑(r1, w0) 2, ⇓(r0, w1) 2, ⇓(r1, w0) 2, ⇕(r0) 1. Sum k = 10.
Total accesses = 10 × 1024 = 10,240. Test time = 10,240 × 5 ns = 51,200 ns = 51.2 µs.
examples.answer: March C− needs 10,240 accesses and 51.2 µs; GALPAT needs 4,194,304 accesses and about 21 ms, 409.6 times longer, so March C− is the production choice.

examples.question: A 4-address bit-oriented memory has an up-inversion coupling fault: whenever cell 2 changes 0 → 1, cell 0 flips. Run March C− and find the first read that fails.
steps: The table gives the contents of cells 0 to 3 after each element; a cell is written in the order the element visits it.
examples.answer: The first fail is the r1 at address 0 in the second element ⇑(r1, w0): the cell reads 0. The fault was excited at address 2 in the first ⇑ element, but it shows only when cell 0 is read again.

head: Element
What happens
Cells 0 1 2 3 after it
rows: address 0: read 0, write 1. Address 1: same. Address 2: read 0, write 1, and the 0 → 1 change flips cell 0 to 0. Address 3: read 0, write 1

traps: Running the middle of March C− with alternating directions (⇑, ⇓, ⇑, ⇓). The standard order is two ascending elements, then two descending. On a 4-cell memory the standard order catches all 72 single coupling faults and all 8 transition faults; the alternating order misses 24 of them, and MATS+ misses 40.
Confusing 10n with 10n². March tests are linear in n; only walking and GALPAT tests are quadratic.
Reading r1 as 'write 1'. r1 reads and expects 1; w1 writes 1.
Testing the array and forgetting the logic around it. Byte enables, ECC and wrap logic can hide or cause failures.
Mixing up words and bits. For a word-wide memory, n counts addresses and each access moves a whole word with a chosen data background.

quiz.q: In a march test, what do n, ⇑ and r0 mean?
quiz.a: n is the number of addresses; ⇑ visits them in ascending order; r0 reads a cell and expects 0.

quiz.q: Write the six elements of March C−.
Why can a stuck-at vector set built for logic miss a coupling fault?
quiz.a: It does not give the victim a known value, write the aggressor with the needed transition and then read the victim, so the disturbance is never caused or never seen.

quiz.q: Name the three address decoder faults.
quiz.a: An address selects no cell; it selects several cells; it selects the wrong cell.

quiz.q: MATS+ and March C− are run on a 256-address memory. How many accesses does each need?
In the second worked example, suppose instead cell 1 has an up-transition fault (it cannot change 0 → 1). Where does March C− first fail?
quiz.a: ⇕(w0) writes 0. In ⇑(r0, w1) the w1 at address 1 leaves it at 0. In ⇑(r1, w0) the r1 at address 1 reads 0: fail, in the second element at address 1.

quiz.q: Why does GALPAT cost about 4n² accesses, and when is it still used?
quiz.a: For each of the n base cells it reads all the other cells, so the work grows with n². It is used on small arrays or to diagnose a failing memory, not in production test of large memories.

beyond: Not for the exam. Large SoC memories are repaired after test: built-in self-repair maps failing rows and columns to spares, stored in fuses. Cars and medical devices run memory BIST at every power-up, and DRAM test now includes row-hammer patterns, where repeated access to one row disturbs its neighbours. Search 'March SS', 'built-in self-repair' and 'row hammer test'.
